subject: Performance SLO & Context Window — follow-up and next steps
messages:
From: Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwood.ai>
To: John Sato <john.sato@finco.com>, Priya Rao <priya.rao@finco.com>
Cc: Vivek Kulkarni <vivek.kulkarni@redwood.ai>
Date: Wed, 25 Feb 2026 14:12:00 -0800
Subject: Performance SLO & Context Window — post-call recap

Hi John / Priya —

Thanks for the call today — really helpful to walk through FinCo's primary flows and the performance targets you're trying to hit. Quick recap and agreed next steps below. Please flag if I missed anything.

Summary of requirements (as discussed):
- Peak request profile: ~50 reqs/sec for the initial phase, expected burst to 120 reqs/sec during month-end reporting.
- Concurrency: 10 steady concurrent sessions per tenant; plan to scale to 25 in Q3.
- Latency SLOs: P95 end-to-end latency target for a typical request (input ~2k tokens, output ~500 tokens) is <= 450 ms. P99 target is <= 800 ms (initial negotiation).
- Streaming: Partial token streaming required for UI responsiveness (first tokens should arrive within ~150–250 ms).
- Context window: most calls will include a historical context of 6–8k tokens (customer transcripts + metadata). A smaller subset (investigations) may need 16k context.
- Quality: you prefer minimal quantization that doesn't degrade NLU for legal text; willing to evaluate 4-bit quantization if evals pass.

Immediate next steps we agreed:
1) I'll send a short technical note on how context window and token sizes map to latency and throughput on our runtime. (Attached: redwood-slo-calc.xlsx and notes.)
2) We'll run a short scoped perf trial: 1 week, 50 reqs/sec steady, 10 concurrency, two model variants (base FP16, 4-bit quantized) — Redwood will provide test harness.
3) Schedule a follow-up tech sync (engineering + infra) to validate networking and burst policy.

Notes on measurement: our platform measures p50/p95/p99 per-route and reports token-level breakdowns (prompt vs. generation). We'll include prefix caching and batching strategies in the perf trial to mirror your production patterns.

I'll schedule the tech sync for next week — proposed times in a follow-up email.

Thanks,
Marissa

marissa.cole@redwood.ai | +1 (415) 555-0127

Attachments: redwood-slo-calc.xlsx (calc sheet with throughput/latency estimates), context-window-latency-notes.pdf (short explainer)

Thanks Marissa — this looks good and matches our notes. Two quick clarifications before we lock the trial:

1) For the streaming requirement, is the 150–250 ms target measured from request arrival at the edge or from request acceptance by the model backend? Our UX team measures from click to first token visible.
2) For the 16k context cases, how much of a latency penalty should we expect relative to 8k? That will determine whether we should route those to a higher-capacity pool or accept a higher SLO.

Also, can you confirm whether your trial harness will simulate our typical pre-processing (PII redaction + anonymization) step — that adds about 30–40 ms per request in our pipeline.

If you can answer those, we'll confirm the trial and send the signed mutual action plan.

Best,

From: Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwood.ai>
To: John Sato <john.sato@finco.com>, Priya Rao <priya.rao@finco.com>
Cc: Vivek Kulkarni <vivek.kulkarni@redwood.ai>
Date: Fri, 27 Feb 2026 10:18:00 -0800
Subject: Re: Performance SLO & Context Window — post-call recap

Great questions — answering inline below. (Putting these in writing so engineering has a clear checklist for the trial.)

1) Streaming measurement baseline
- UX measurement (click → first token visible) is the right customer-facing metric. For our internal SLOs we typically measure from our edge ingress to first token emitted by the runtime; the end-to-end UX figure will include your pre-processing and network hop.
- For planning, assume: client pre-processing (your anonymization) ~35 ms, network (round-trip) ~60–120 ms depending on region, Redwood edge-to-runtime and tokenization ~30–60 ms. So if your UX target is first token <= 250 ms, we need runtime to emit first token within ~100–150 ms from request acceptance. We'll validate this during the trial.

2) Context window impact (8k → 16k)
- Latency impact is dominated by two things: the encoder/attention pass over the full context and KV cache size/lookup costs during generation. For decoder-only models we still pay an initial cost roughly O(n^2) in practice when the model processes very long inputs (long context attention), though optimized runtimes and attention approximations reduce this.
- Empirical estimates (on Redwood Dedicated nodes with A100/H100-class GPUs):
  • 8k input + 512 output: baseline P95 for first-token generation ≈ 120–180 ms (runtime-only).
  • 16k input + 512 output: baseline P95 increases to ≈ 220–360 ms (runtime-only), so roughly ~1.8–2.0x on first-token.
  • Ongoing token emissions (streaming) scale approximately linearly with output length; large input increases memory + KV access overhead but per-output-token time impact is smaller than the initial cost.
- Practical recommendation: route 16k-context heavy flows to a higher-memory pool (larger batch size tolerance and higher per-request GPU allocation) if you want to preserve the same P95 budget as 8k flows. Alternatively, allow a higher SLO for those investigative queries.

3) Throughput and batching trade-offs
- Continuous batching improves GPU utilization and reduces tokens-per-cost, but it increases tail latency when batch windows accumulate. For your P95 targets we recommend:
  • Target steady-state batching window of 8–15 ms for chat-like workloads (keeps p95 low).
  • Use adaptive burst policies to allow slightly larger batching (30–50 ms) during background bulk jobs.
- For the perf trial we'll run with two batching configs so you can see the latency/throughput trade-offs.

4) Concurrency / autoscale
- For the initial phase (10 concurrent sessions, 50 reqs/sec) we expect a single dedicated pool of 4–6 GPUs (H100-class) will meet p95=450 ms for 2k/500 token profiles, depending on model variant. We'll size the trial cluster conservatively and provide queuing metrics so you can set autoscale rules.

5) Quantization and quality
- 4-bit quantization can reduce memory and improve throughput by ~1.6–2x, but there's a risk of subtle quality regressions on legal text. We'll run your eval set during the trial and gate 4-bit rollout on your quality thresholds.

6) Pre-processing overhead
- We'll include a pre-processing shim in the trial harness to represent your 35 ms anonymization step so the end-to-end numbers we report match your UX measurements.

Next actions from us:
- Redwood: deliver trial harness + two model variants + two batching configs. Share initial sizing plan. (Attached: redwood-slo-calc.xlsx)
- FinCo: sign the scoped trial MOU and provide anonymized sample payloads (up to 1k requests).

I'll follow up with a proposed tech sync slot. Thanks — happy to jump on a call with your infra folks to go over networking and egress.

— Marissa

Subject: Fwd: Performance SLO & Context Window — follow-up and next steps

Looping in our infra lead (I'll include offline) — John and Priya asked for two concrete options for the trial cluster (cost/latency tradeoffs). I'm proposing we surface:
A) Cost-optimized: 4x H100, aggressive batching → better throughput, slightly higher P95 for streaming-first-token.
B) Latency-optimized: 6x H100, minimal batching, KV cache warmed per session → preserves first-token p95 under 200 ms for 8k contexts.

Marissa — please confirm you want both options in the sizing doc and I will ask infra to prepare cost estimates and a short runbook for cache warm-up. Also adding the link to the HubSpot deal in the notes.
